coding_note: Home ownership: OR 1.31 for piped-water interruption (higher = worse). Raw sign +, substantive Unfavourable: the tenure-security hypothesis predicts fewer interruptions.

comparator_full: Non-owner households (renters/other tenure).
estimate_full: Home ownership associated with higher odds of reporting water-supply interruption (OR=1.31, p<0.01), controlling for provider and other household/neighbourhood covariates; overall 47% (95% CI 45-49%) of piped households reported >=1 full day of unavailability in the prior fortnight, ranging 18-76% across providers.

estimate_short: significant reduction (neg. binomial IRR; CI in supplement)
coding_note: Reported contrast is unincorporated vs incorporated (significantly reduced access). Restated to incorporated vs unincorporated the association is positive: Favourable for recognition.
raw_direction_text: negative (unincorporated/unrecognized jurisdictional status associated with reduced service access)
exposure_full: Municipal incorporation status (incorporated vs. unincorporated), which functions as the legal/jurisdictional eligibility gateway to centralized municipal water/wastewater service extension in the U.S.
comparator_full: Incorporated census block groups.
estimate_full: Unincorporated status and poverty rate are significantly associated with reduced centralized water/wastewater infrastructure access; sewer coverage rates significantly lower for unincorporated communities near municipal boundaries, consistent with municipal underbounding excluding these areas from service-area expansion. Full-text check 2026-10-04 (main text; the confidence intervals are in Supplementary Tables 5-6, which are not in the PDF): among high-poverty block groups, unincorporated status is associated with 3.54 times the unsewered land area and 17.8 times the area unserved by centralized water (incidence rate ratios); among block groups without high poverty, 1.48 times the unsewered area; for high-poverty Outlying and Island communities the IRR for unsewered area exceeds 4.0, while Outlying communities without high poverty have IRR 0.91.

coding_note: Own metered connection: +27.2% consumption, +0.35 SD cleanliness, ORs 2.16 (ease) and 2.76 (affordable expenses).

exposure_full: Household formal connection status to the municipal water utility (Baguio Water District, BWD): own household metered connection, requiring an upfront PHP 10,000-14,000 (US$234-327) connection fee plus installation cost.
comparator_full: Households with no BWD connection (referent category); a shared/other BWD connection category also modeled.
estimate_full: Own household BWD connection vs. none: +27.2% increase in reported liters-per-capita-per-day consumption; +0.35 SD in perceived-cleanliness PCA score; 2.16x odds of reporting extreme ease of water access; 2.76x odds of reporting affordable water expenses (all coefficients statistically significant at conventional thresholds per reported asterisks). coding_note: Water-user-association management: piped-water access about 6 pp above trend (DiD with kernel matching).
raw_direction_text: positive and significant (WUA/participatory management increases piped-water access rates)
exposure_full: Rural municipality implements a small-scale water supply system through a community-based water user association (WUA) -- a participatory institutional/legal management model -- versus
comparator_full: Rural municipality implements a small-scale water supply system through non-participatory local government management (the referent/control project type).
estimate_full: Municipalities with WUA-managed projects realized piped-water access-rate increases of approximately 6 percentage points above the national average trend (statistically significant, robust to specification changes and matching-balance checks). Rural piped-water access rose from a 15-16% baseline (2000) to 33.4% in WUA-served areas versus 24.9% in local-government-served areas by 2010. Heterogeneity analysis: in local-government-project municipalities with independently higher accountability (local media presence, political competition, or pre-implementation citizen mobilization), access-rate gains matched WUA-area gains, indicating participatory accountability -- not project type per se -- is the underlying mechanism.
ck_comment: the exposure is a community-based water-user-association management model for small systems against municipal management: community management and programme delivery, with no access rule tested (the A24 Group 3 pattern)

coding_note: Usos y costumbres: ATT 0.086 on sewerage access (PSM-DiD).

comparator_full: Party-governed municipalities in Oaxaca, Mexico (n=146 control, over common support after kernel-density propensity-score matching on municipal characteristics and long-term settlement patterns).
estimate_full: Sewerage access ATT = 0.086 (level, 1995-2005, p<0.01), and 9.05 percentage-point ATT in rate of change (1995-2005, p<0.01); smaller but still positive effect for 2000-10. Piped-water-access ATT was small and not statistically significant across all periods examined (e.g. 1990-2010 level ATT = 0.027, p=0.595).

Model fit: NGO model pseudo R2=0.4381; CBO model pseudo R2=0.2631 (both Wald chi2 p<0.001).

outcome_short: equity of unit price and cost recovery
coding_note: Urban (si) status and tax burden go with lower inequity coefficients; fiscal independence goes with a higher one.
raw_direction_text: mixed: administrative si classification and local tax burden per person are associated with GREATER equity (lower inequity coefficient); municipal fiscal autonomy (financial independence) is associated with LESS equity (higher inequity coefficient)
exposure_full: Administrative district legal/institutional classification (si, urban-type, coded 1) versus gun (rural-type, coded 0) among South Korean local governments, 2010/2016/2021, alongside municipal fiscal autonomy (degree of financial independence, i.e. own-source revenue share of general accounting revenue) and local tax burden per person (log).
comparator_full: Gun (rural-type) administrative districts as the reference category for the si/gun coefficient; lower financial independence and lower local tax burden per person as the implicit comparison for the fiscal coefficients, within the same 152-local-government sample.
estimate_full: Administrative district unit (si=1): significant NEGATIVE coefficient (improves equity) in 2021 on average unit price (-0.9174, p<0.01), cost-recovery rate (-0.9064, p<0.05), revenue-water ratio (-0.8489, p<0.05), water-supply rate (-0.8566, p<0.01), and number of employees (-1.1569, p<0.01); not significant for customer satisfaction. Degree of financial independence: significant POSITIVE coefficient (worsens equity) on all 6 variables at p<0.01 in all 3 years (e.g. average unit price 2021: 0.1353). Local tax burden per person (log): significant NEGATIVE coefficient (improves equity) on all 6 variables at p<0.01 in all 3 years (e.g. average unit price 2021: -1.9115). Coefficients were consistent in sign and significance pattern across 2010, 2016, and 2021, and robust to an ordinary-multiple-regression sensitivity check.

raw_direction_text: negative (local government proliferation associated with LOWER household water/sanitation access, relative to original non-split districts)
exposure_full: Creation of a new local government (kabupaten/kota) via pemekaran -- the legal/administrative splitting of an existing district jurisdiction into smaller administrative units -- in Indonesia's post-2001 decentralization era, exploiting the plausibly exogenous timing of district-splitting decisions as the identifying exposure.
comparator_full: Original (non-split) parent districts, and separately, sibling split-off districts, all within the same national panel of 336 kabupaten/kota, 2001-2014.
estimate_full: New-district creation reduces household access to protected water and sanitation by approximately 1% in year 2 relative to original districts (static DiD model) and by approximately 1.35 percentage points in the second year of operation (dynamic GMM model), implying a long-run reduction of approximately 1.75% (beta/(1-gamma) = -1.35/(1-0.23)), p=.023. No significant contemporaneous or lagged effect relative to split-off (sibling) districts, and no significant effect on school enrollment in either comparison. Falsification tests using first and second leads of the new-district dummy show no significant pre-trend, supporting the parallel-trends assumption.

coding_note: Private ownership: +0.3456 R$/m3 on the tariff level (higher = worse). Raw sign +, substantive Unfavourable.
raw_direction_text: positive (private ownership associated with HIGHER water tariffs, i.e. lower affordability, relative to public/mixed-capital ownership; overall and unregulated clusters only)
exposure_full: Private (vs. public) ownership of a Brazilian water and sanitation business corporation -- a governance-structure/institutional variable -- tested alongside presence/type of economic regulatory agency (local vs. regional vs. unregulated) and regulatory regime (rate-of-return, price-cap/revenue-cap, vs. municipally-negotiated tariff).
comparator_full: Publicly-owned and mixed-capital Brazilian water/sanitation corporations within the same unbalanced panel, 51 business corporations (22 private, remainder public/mixed-capital), 2005-2012.
estimate_full: Private-ownership (Priv) coefficient +0.3456 R$/m3 on the water-tariff-level model (Lwt), significant in the overall and unregulated clusters; not significant within the regulated-only cluster. Local/regional regulatory-agency coefficients negative but not significant (H2 rejected). Rate-of-return and price-cap/revenue-cap regulatory-regime coefficients not significant relative to municipally-negotiated tariffs (H3 rejected).

exposure_short: Random contract enforcement: credible disconnection notices (Kenya)
coding_note: Credible disconnection notices: +30 pp payment compliance (a utility-side outcome), null on water access, connections, spending and collection time. Kept as Mixed by the author (A26); a sensitivity scenario (S4e) treats household water access alone as Null.
raw_direction_text: positive and significant for payment compliance; null (no significant effect) for water access, connection rates, spending and collection time
exposure_full: Randomized assignment to systematic contract enforcement (transparent, credible service-disconnection notices for nonpayment, per the terms of the property owner's utility connection-loan contract), Nairobi informal settlements.
comparator_full: Disconnection-eligible control compounds exempted from enforcement (ad hoc/no systematic disconnection).
estimate_full: Payment likelihood within one month increased by 30 percentage points from an 11-percentage-point control base (p<0.001); total payments increased by US$8.80 from a US$5.02 base (p<0.001). Water-access outcomes at 9-month endline: piped water/sanitation connection rates statistically indistinguishable between treatment and control (most of 96 disconnected compounds reconnected after partial payment); main water source = piped water 4.4 percentage points higher in treatment, not significant (p=0.243); monthly water spending Control US$6.62 vs Treatment US$6.86 (p=0.803); weekly water-collection time Control 118 min vs Treatment 100 min (p=0.388) -- a precisely estimated null effect of contract enforcement on actual household water access.

coding_note: Regulation quality: coefficient 0.0121 on access to drinking water.
raw_direction_text: positive (higher institutional/regulatory quality associated with greater water/sanitation access and smaller urban-rural gap)
exposure_full: Higher institutional/regulatory governance quality (World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators 'regulation quality' index) at the national level, in the presence of natural-resource-rent dependence, across 44 African countries, 1995-2017.
comparator_full: Countries/country-years with lower regulation-quality index scores, within the same 44-country dynamic panel.
estimate_full: Regulation quality has a positive, statistically significant direct effect on access to drinking water for the total population (coefficient = 0.0121, p<0.01) and significantly reduces the urban-rural water-access gap (coefficient = -0.0511, p<0.01); broadly consistent significant effects are found for sanitation access. Separately, democratic institutional quality is shown to mitigate the negative resource-curse effect of natural-resource-rent dependence on water/sanitation access.
ck_comment: the exposure is the national World Bank regulation-quality index across 44 countries: macro-governance, as in S348 and S969 (excluded E03, effect rows removed)

coding_note: The reported contrast is state-regulated minus locally regulated welfare loss (-4.6 pp; higher = worse), so the exposure is state PUC regulation. effect_sizes.csv carried the opposite pole in its exposure_definition until the author's A26 ruling of 2026-10-14, which swapped exposure and comparator to match.
raw_direction_text: negative (state-level economic regulation associated with lower excess pricing / lower monopoly welfare loss, i.e., improved affordability, relative to local-only regulation)
exposure_full: Residential customers of a municipally-owned water utility subject to state public utility commission (PUC) economic regulation (in the five U.S. states that regulated municipal water rate structures at the state level), United States, 1965 AWWA survey data.
comparator_full: Residential customers of a municipally-owned water utility subject to local-only economic regulation (regulated by city council or water commission, not by a state public utility commission).
estimate_full: Model 1 (unweighted average): locally-regulated 9.6% (SE 0.583, n=88) vs. state-regulated 5.2% (SE 0.818, n=27); difference -4.6 percentage points, t=-4.58 (p<0.01, one-tailed). Model 2 (weighted average): locally-regulated 10.39% (SE 0.786) vs. state-regulated 6.15% (SE 1.35); difference -4.24 percentage points, t=-2.71 (p<0.01, one-tailed).

coding_note: Inverted U: positive coefficient on cost recovery, negative on its square.
raw_direction_text: positive up to a threshold, then negative (curvilinear/inverted-U)
exposure_full: Water-utility operation-and-maintenance (O&M) cost-recovery ratio (a financial/regulatory institutional-policy mechanism), and its square, across Sub-Saharan African water utilities.
comparator_full: Utility-years within the same panel with lower cost-recovery ratios.
estimate_full: O&M cost-recovery ratio (cr): positive, significant coefficient on coverage change across all specifications. Squared term (cr^2): negative, significant coefficient of comparable magnitude -- curvilinear (inverted-U) relationship; coverage gains from cost recovery diminish and reverse beyond a threshold level. Exact numeric coefficient/SE values in source Table 4 were not cleanly extractable from PDF-to-text conversion (table structure garbled); direction and significance are drawn from the paper's own prose description of its regression results (Section 4).

exposure_short: Political capture: Gram Panchayat head's village or politician's road (India)
outcome_directness_check: checked 2026-10-14: no household access measure; kept by the author (A26)

raw_direction_text: positive (political proximity increases sanitation-infrastructure provision; SC/ST residence decreases it)
exposure_full: Political capture of village sanitation infrastructure: residing in the Gram Panchayat head's village, or on a road where a politician resides, vs. other village roads; road inhabited predominantly by Scheduled Castes/Tribes vs. upper-caste road; 5,276 villages/wards, 10,408 roads, 4 South Indian states.

coding_note: Regional utilities corruption: negative marginal effect on reporting enough clean water.
raw_direction_text: negative (higher regional utilities-sector corruption reduces likelihood of reported adequate household water access)
exposure_full: Regional incidence of utilities-sector corruption (Afrobarometer round 7, multi-country Africa sample), measured as the share of households in a region reporting corruption experiences with utilities officials.
comparator_full: Households in regions with lower/zero reported utilities-sector corruption incidence, holding piped-water-system presence, urban/rural location, gender, and country fixed effects constant.
estimate_full: Regional utilities corruption has a statistically significant negative marginal effect on the likelihood a household reports access to enough clean water (Table 2), robust to controlling for individual bribery experience and confirmed in an ordered-probit specification (Table 3, N=44,778). A household in the most-corrupt sampled area is approximately 10% less likely to report adequate water access than one in the cleanest area; a one-standard-deviation increase in the corruption measure is associated with an approximate 0.5% drop in reported access likelihood.
ck_comment: the exposure is the regional incidence of utilities-sector corruption (a governance-quality measure, cf. S348) rather than a rule or mechanism of access

coding_note: Price-regulated provider: coefficient -1.19, about 27 pp lower probability that a colonia had water service.

exposure_full: The colonia's water provider is subject to price (rate) regulation (municipal systems under their own rate-setting, county systems and districts under the state environmental commission), as opposed to providers whose rates are not regulated (non-profit water supply corporations and for-profit suppliers); Texas law does not mandate universal service.

estimate_full: Price-regulated provider: coefficient -1.1858 (SE 0.4163, p = 0.004), marginal effect -0.2718, about 27 percentage points lower probability that a colonia had water service by 1996. Access to Rural Development funding 0.2162 (p = 0.401); county cited for lax enforcement of the model subdivision rules -7.5722 (p = 0.004), marginal effect -0.6943; median per capita income +0.1410 (p = 0.001). Model A (provider type against private for-profit): municipal -1.9433 (p = 0.051), district or county -1.1105 (p = 0.035), non-profit corporation -0.3795 (p = 0.535), wells or unknown -2.3819 (p = 0.007). The author reads this as rate regulation, intended to make service affordable, possibly reducing coverage among the poor.
